activities.caption: file each lever by its clock
activities.name: madClockBuckets

config.prompt: Two clocks run the mitigation ledger — file each lever:

items.label: methane — decade-scale lifetime, ~80× CO₂'s warming per kilogram over 20 years
oil-and-gas leak repairs, landfill gas, livestock feeds
cement's process CO₂ released from limestone itself

config.why: Fast methane cuts are the near-term lever; slow CO₂ elimination is the commitment-determining one — confusing them is the most common quantitative error in the public debate.

activities.anchor: One worked calculation shows why electrification is the design keystone
activities.caption: call the saving — boiler vs heat pump
activities.name: madHeatPumpEstimate

config.prompt: A gas boiler delivers heat at ~90% efficiency. A heat pump with a coefficient of performance of 3 moves heat instead of making it. Roughly how much less energy does the heat pump use for the same warmth?
config.why: A COP of 3 means a third of the energy for the same heat: 1/3 ÷ (1/0.9) ≈ 0.3 — about 70% less, even before the grid cleans.
config.context: Every clean megawatt-hour decarbonises whichever loads have been electrified onto it — progressively and permanently.

config.root: A company pledges 'net zero by 2040' while its reported emissions keep rising. You are auditing the pledge.

start.text: What decides whether the pledge is real?

choices.label: Are removals counted against residuals — or against avoided cuts?
choices.feedback: The central question of the whole audit.

choices.label: Are the remaining sources genuinely hard — agriculture, aviation, cement process CO₂?
choices.feedback: That is exactly what removals are reserved for.

choices.label: Is the logo green enough?
choices.feedback: Presentation is not where pledges fail.

arbiter.text: Removals counted against avoided cuts is the failure mode; removals counted against residuals is the design.

residual.text: Then permanent removals are legitimately in play — that is where the last, hardest trillions are spent.

greenwash.text: Claiming removals for emissions that could simply have been cut is the precise greenwash the distinction guards against.

config.why: Net zero means residuals balanced by removals, not a ban on combustion — and absolutism fails the same arithmetic as greenwash.

activities.caption: stack the wedges in deployment order
activities.name: madWedgeOrder

config.prompt: The mitigation portfolio, as the lesson ranks it — put the wedges in order:
items: Electricity leads: solar and wind (module prices fell roughly 90% in the 2010s) plus storage and transmission
Electrification converts transport and building heat to that clean supply
Methane cuts form the fast wedge, buying near-term time
Industry — steel, cement, chemicals — the stubborn wedges needing hydrogen, CCS or new chemistry
config.why: The gap arithmetic: current policies land ~2.5–3 °C; 1.5 °C requires roughly 43–45% cuts by 2030 — the tools exist, and the deployment is behind.

activities.anchor: locates agency where the abatement is not largest
activities.caption: bet before you read on — where the levers live
activities.name: madAgencyPredict

config.q: The 'personal carbon footprint' framing was popularised, ironically, by a fossil company's 2000s campaign. What did it do to the agency question?
choices: Put it where the abatement is largest — every bit adds up
Moved it away from the binding levers — the grid, codes, vehicles, prices
config.why: The binding levers are systemic; individuals vote, invest, build and advocate their way into the systemic wedges — and household changes are exactly the demand signal those wedges need.

activities.anchor: even a full nuclear build-out leaves the same set
activities.caption: find the faulty line — the hero-technology plan
activities.name: madHeroSpot

config.prompt: A politician's energy plan contains one faulty line — click it:
lines: Our nation will pick the one hero technology and decarbonise with it.
The costs are regional: Iceland geothermal, Morocco solar, Norway hydro.
Since renewables alone cannot reach net zero, we should dismiss them entirely.
Wedge thinking exists to prevent both the single-technology error and its mirror.
No single wedge reaches net zero — industry, aviation, shipping, agriculture and removals remain either way.
config.correction: No wedge is worthless because it cannot do everything — the honest portfolio question is which wedges are cheapest where.
config.why: Wedge thinking prevents the hero error and, equally, the fatalism that writes off a tool for not solving the whole problem.

activities.caption: pair each design rule with its reason
activities.name: madAcidMatch

config.prompt: What cap-and-trade taught the carbon market — pair rule with reason:

pairs.right: a 'rate' standard lets growth eat the gains
stack sensors fed a public registry
cheaper than central guesses — the flexibility was worth billions
the cap must eventually reach zero, not merely a percentage down

config.why: Emissions fell about half within a decade with near-total compliance — absolute cap, tradeable permits, verified monitoring, sources spanning the whole economy rather than one industry.

activities.anchor: Why the template transfers only partially to climate
activities.caption: fill the blanks — the protocol's machinery
activities.name: madOzoneCloze

config.text: The Montreal Protocol achieved %%0%% ratification — the first treaty in UN history to do so — with binding phase-out schedules, a %%1%% paying developing countries' compliance costs, and amendment machinery that tightened as science advanced. The %%2%% amendment (2016) now phases down HFCs, the CFC substitutes that turned out to be potent greenhouse gases.
config.hint: The lessons that do transfer: bind before certainty is total, fund the transition, build ratchet cycles.
